explanation: An owl's 14 neck vertebrae help it swivel its head about 270 degrees. A giraffe has 7, the same number as a human; each one is just far longer.

claims.text: Owls can turn their heads up to about 270 degrees.
Each giraffe neck vertebra is much longer than a human neck vertebra.

writerNotes: Self-check (guide 9.3), all eleven codes confirmed true. The selfCheck field itself is left out because the CNT-1 item schema refuses it as an unknown key, so the codes are recorded here. lint: content:check reports no errors and no warnings for this item. claims: five listed; c1 to c4 hold numbers, so they are high by the C26 floor. One search on owl and giraffe neck vertebrae should cover c1 to c4 together. datasets: no pinned dataset in content/datasets/manifest.json covers animal or plant biology, so none applies and every high-risk claim needs web evidence from checker A. rivalTest: the giraffe is the obvious pick, which is why counterintuitive is set. Exact counts, so the separation guard is met many times over (14 against 7). Many birds have more than 7 neck vertebrae and swans more than owls, which is why the stem compares only these two. volatility: evergreen, a settled fact that cannot change; no time words, and nothing rests on knowledge newer than mid-2026. regional: owls and giraffes are known everywhere. style: Oxford spelling, plain hyphens only, explanation of 29 words. myths: screened against content/reference/myths.json; no entry matches. mystery and encore: nothing of either kind in a comparison item. doubts: none; 14 for owls and 7 for giraffes are standard anatomy figures.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Giraffes have seven cervical vertebrae, the same count as most mammals. Evidence on the phylogenetic constraint to the number of cervical vertebrae in mammals suggests that the giraffe has 7 cervical vertebrae. The neck's length comes from much longer vertebrae, not extra ones ... One study had proposed eight, but the mainstream count is seven.

claimResults.note: Stated plainly. The study that 'proposed eight' argued that the giraffe's first thoracic vertebra works like a neck vertebra; it does not change the count of cervical vertebrae the claim names, and the owl wins either way (14 against 8). Noted as an issue. W12, counted here, said only that giraffes are 'generally thought' to have seven, so it is not used for this claim.
